headline: The Point Splits in Two: Blues Own the Bunker, Bass Own the Dark
subhead: A neap tide softens the rips this week, stretching the low-light bass window while daytime bluefish carve up bunker schools off the Lighthouse.
body_markdown:
Every July the Point splits into two different fisheries, and this week it's split clean down the middle. By day it belongs to the bluefish — bunker schools rolling past the Lighthouse in tight, nervous balls, blues underneath them cutting through like a chainsaw through a two-by-four. By dark, it belongs to the bass, and if you've fished this rock long enough you know that's exactly how it's supposed to go in high summer. This isn't decline. This is the rhythm the Point has kept for as long as anyone's been keeping records on it.

Water off the Lighthouse is holding around 69 degrees, which is comfortable enough to keep bait stacked tight to structure without pushing everything offshore into deep water. That's the number that matters right now — warm enough to hold bunker schools along the beach and out past North Bar, cool enough that the better striped bass haven't abandoned ship for cooler water up the Cape or into the Race. What it's done instead is push the bulk of the keeper-class bass into a nocturnal pattern. Dawn, dusk, and full dark — that's the window. Midday sun on 69-degree water and a stripers' metabolism just doesn't line up the way it did in May.

The rips are still the show. North Bar on the building tide has been giving up bass in the 20 to 34-inch range to guys working bucktails — 1.5 to 2-ounce white or chartreuse, bounced hard off the bottom on the downcurrent side where the sand drops into the trough. Cast up-current, let it sink clean to the bottom before you start working it, and keep contact through the swing. That's the Point pattern, always has been. Eels are still money after dark — rigged eels drifted through Shagwong Reef on the first two hours of the outgoing, and live eels worked off the boulder field on the south side for guys willing to fish the tide change at 4 a.m. I had a report of a bass pushing 38 pounds taken off the south side rocks on a live eel just after midnight last Thursday — that's the kind of fish this rock still produces when you put the time in and fish it right, in the dark, with nobody else around.

Daytime, if you want action instead of patience, the bluefish are doing exactly what bunker schools moving along the beach have been forcing them to do coastwide this month — and Montauk's getting its share as those pods work their way east. Diamond jigs, 3 to 4 ounces, worked through the surface froth when the blues are up busting bait, or a bucktail with a pork rind trailer bounced through the edges when they've gone under. Turtle Cove and the rip line running off the Lighthouse itself have both been holding these bluefish blitzes at various points through the week — nothing subtle about it, you'll see the birds and the surface chop from half a mile out. Bring wire or heavy fluoro leader, because these fish are shredding light mono without even trying.

With the bass on a low-light clock and the blues owning the noon hour, porgies and sea bass on Shagwong Reef have become the smart daytime move for anyone who wants fish in the cooler without burning a tide waiting for dark. Standard high-low rigs, squid strips or clam, over the reef structure in 30 to 50 feet — it's not glamorous but it's about as close to a sure thing as this Point offers right now, and it fills the hours between the real bite windows.

Fluke drifts off the south side and out toward the Elbow have been steady if not spectacular — 3 to 4-ounce bucktails tipped with Gulp Swimming Mullet in white or pink, dragged slow along the sand-to-structure transitions where the current sweeps bait off the reef edges. Keepers are mixed in with plenty of shorts, so it's a numbers game more than a guaranteed box, but it's a fine way to spend a slack tide between the bass windows.

We flagged the tuna building offshore last week, and the canyon boats running out of Montauk Harbor are confirming it — yellowfin and bigeye activity improving as this stable, high-pressure stretch holds warm water in range out toward the canyons. If you've got a canyon trip on the books, this is the stretch to use it.

The moon goes first-quarter this week, which means we're sliding into neap tides — softer current through the rips at Shagwong and North Bar than you'll see at the new or full moon. That's not bad news. Softer current actually widens the productive window for eel and bucktail presentations beyond the peak of the tide, so you don't have to thread as tight a needle timing your trip. What it also means is the first false albacore and bonito scouts — which typically show around the Point in that late-July stretch as water keeps climbing — haven't announced themselves yet. Keep an eye on temperature breaks out past the Point and around the Elbow over the next week or two. When the water firms up another degree or two and the bait compresses, that's when the first albie showing usually happens out here, and it can happen fast once it starts.

For now: fish the low light for bass, fish the bunker schools for blues, and use the reef for porgies when the sun's too high for anything else. That's the Point in late July. It's not complicated, but it does ask you to show up when most people are asleep.
